TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Intervenor Jason A. Howton files this brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 under SOAH Order No. 35. The Commission remanded only those two issues. This brief stays inside them. It does not ask the ALJs to reopen the record. Its factual statements cite admitted exhibits, the certified hearing transcript, and the Proposal for Decision (PFD). It cites Commission and SOAH orders, party pleadings, and governing law as what they are. SOAH Order No. 35 treats Applicants' Directory of Evidence as their early-filed brief, and this brief answers it on the record the Directory leaves out.
I.	SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Commission asked two plain questions. Issue No. 11 asks whether "the proposed transmission facilities" are "necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards." Issue No. 13 asks what congestion cost savings "may result from the proposed transmission facilities." The Chairman put the point directly: the question is whether the facilities "are in fact necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, not how the applicants characterize the project."
The answer to both questions turns on one fact. No study in this record compares system performance with and without the Bell County East to Big Hill facilities (with the Big Hill to Sand Lake facilities, "Import Path 2") and identifies a specific thermal, voltage, stability, or contingency violation attributable to their absence. ERCOT's Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) sized the 765-kV import paths for 2038 load and considered only a 345-kV import path for 2030. ERCOT then told the Commission that two of the three 765-kV paths, not all three, are needed by 2030. The 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans (RTPs), on which Applicants rest the 2030 date, started with all three paths already in the model. Applicants' witness testified that he knew of no study that isolated each line, and that he "assume[d]" this line was needed because all of them were said to be needed together. A standard that is met by assumption has not been tested. Applicants say as much in their own reply to Intervenor's exceptions: their planning models "assume that the Import Path 2 Projects are in service."
The load that sized the 765-kV option does not survive the ALJs' own findings. The ALJs found that ERCOT's adjusted forecasting method removes at least 3,571 MW from the PBRP's non-oil-and-gas load. That one reduction is larger than the entire safe loading limit of the line before the ALJs, and it carries the 2038 forecast below the 2030 level for which ERCOT studied only 345-kV import paths. New Permian generation, and large loads that now supply themselves, push the same direction. No study in the record determines whether a third import path remains necessary once those facts are counted.
On the federal question the Chairman raised, the answer comes from the statute itself. A NERC reliability standard "does not include any requirement to enlarge such facilities or to construct new transmission capacity or generation capacity." TPL-001-5.1 requires a corrective action plan when a planning assessment finds a deficiency, and it lets that plan take many forms. Declining to certify these facilities would not, by itself, establish or cause a violation of a federal reliability standard.
On Issue No. 13, Applicants chose to stand on the reliability label and offered no estimate of congestion savings from these facilities. Every figure in the Directory compares one statewide plan to another. Once the reliability label falls, PURA § 37.056(d) requires findings comparing the cost of these facilities to consumers with their congestion savings. This record contains the evidence for neither half of that comparison. The ALJs should answer Issue No. 11 "no," answer Issue No. 13 by finding that the record contains no estimate, revise FoF No. 225, and reaffirm the recommendation to deny the applications.
II.	PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11: THE RECORD DOES NOT SHOW THAT THESE FACILITIES ARE NECESSARY TO MEET STATE OR FEDERAL RELIABILITY STANDARDS.
A.	Applicants name the standards ERCOT followed but identify no violation these facilities cure.
Most of the Directory's Issue No. 11 entries say that ERCOT's studies "were performed based on" NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, the ERCOT Protocols, and the ERCOT Planning Criteria, and then list the contingency categories ERCOT simulated. That tells the ALJs how ERCOT studied the system. It does not identify a thermal, voltage, or stability violation, in a named study case and year, that would occur without these facilities and that these facilities resolve. The ALJs have already found that "NERC contingencies can and should influence ERCOT's overarching regional planning, but they are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for Import Path 2." The Directory does not supply that project-specific showing. It cannot, because the studies it cites were not built to make it.
B.	No study isolated these facilities, and Applicants' witnesses filled the gap with an assumption.
The only hearing testimony the Directory cites on Issue No. 11 is Mr. Gurley's answer to whether any partial build study asked if the needs could be met without this line. He answered:
I am not aware that -- aware of a study that isolated each line independently as they were -- they were studied together. In my belief, that's partially due to the requirements under TPL-001, the NERC requirement for this, that requires N minus 1 and N minus 1, minus 1 studies. So you have to be able to remove an element during this study. So I assume, you know, that that leads into part of the recommendation for multiple lines.
That is a belief about why ERCOT recommended several lines. It is not evidence that TPL-001-5.1 requires this line rather than some other combination. Moments earlier, Mr. Gurley agreed that the PBRP placed Import Path 2 in the 2038 solution, that the 2030 date he relied on applied "collectively" to all import paths, and that the plans did not say this individual line was necessary. Asked about this line specifically, he answered: "Well, I would assume by saying that all of them are needed, that this line is needed with them." The ALJs relied on the same testimony in finding that Applicants "had not performed a partial build study to justify Import Path 2 individually."
Applicants' other planning witness stood on the same ground. Mr. Martin testified that the 765-kV import paths are part of ERCOT's exit strategy for the Far West import constraints. On cross-examination he agreed that he did not author that study, and when asked whether he personally ran the power flow or contingency studies behind it, he answered: "We did not run the power flows that produce those." He then explained that Applicants rely on ERCOT's studies, the two RTPs, and "the experiences on the system." Neither witness identified a study that removes this line and records a violation.
C.	ERCOT sized these facilities for 2038 and named two import paths, not three, for 2030.
The PBRP is the document that created Import Path 2. It states: "As noted above, for 2030, ERCOT considered only a 345-kV import path option." The Directory itself quotes the PBRP's statement that "[t]he 765-kV import path option was evaluated for the 2038 Permian Basin region load level." The PBRP modeled 23,659 MW of Permian Basin demand for 2030 and 26,400 MW for 2038. The 765-kV import paths were the answer to the larger number.
ERCOT then told the Commission how to sequence the plan. Its December 12, 2024 letter, admitted as JKK Panel Ex. 01, states that "ERCOT recommends that projects needed to serve the forecasted 2030 load in the Permian Basin Region should be prioritized over projects needed to serve the 2038 load," and that "[t]wo of the four 345-kV import paths and two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030." The ALJs read that letter as "essentially conceding that Import Path 2 was unnecessary through that point in time." Mr. Gurley acknowledged that the spreadsheet attached to the letter "listed 2038 as the year when the reliability need started to appear for all three 765 kV import paths." He added that "at that time, ERCOT was still evaluating the 765 kV and 345 kV alternatives."
Applicants answer that the 2024 RTP later showed Import Path 2 in a "765-kV Core Plan needed in 2030." But that plan did not test whether the line is needed. It began with the line, as Section II.D shows. The ALJs have already found that "[t]he evidence did not establish that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030 to serve the forecasted 2030 load in the Permian Basin region." A supplemental finding on Issue No. 11 should address the Sequencing Letter directly and state the first study year, if any, in which a violation attributable to the absence of these facilities appears. The record does not supply that year.
D.	The 2024 and 2025 RTPs assumed these facilities rather than testing them.
The 2024 RTP says how its 765-kV plan was built: "The start case for the 765-kV plan incorporated all local projects needed by 2030 in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, along with the three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths." ERCOT "began by developing a holistic 765-kV plan" and then picked out the parts it called the core plan. The 2025 RTP did the same. It "included the entire 765-kV STEP in its 2030 and 2031 starting base cases" and "did not see a need to change or remove any element of the 765-kV STEP."
A case that starts with a facility in service cannot show what happens without it. Applicants concede the point in their own words. In their exceptions they described "ERCOT's recommendation in the 2025 RTP, which depends on the Import Path 2 Projects being in service," and said that "no party has studied or validated a reliability solution with those facilities removed from the model." Applicants carry the burden of proof in this case. A study that has never been run is a gap in Applicants' proof, not in anyone else's.
The 2025 RTP also applied ERCOT's adjusted load forecast, which the ALJs relied on in declining to give the PBRP recommendation great weight. The record does not show that the 2025 RTP evaluated the system with these facilities removed under that adjusted load. Keeping an assumed facility in a later case is not a finding that the facility is needed.
E.	The load that sized the 765-kV option does not survive the ALJs' own findings.
The Commission gives great weight to an ERCOT reliability recommendation only when the forecasted load growth is "substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth." The ALJs have already measured how much of the PBRP load meets that test. The table below places the ALJs' findings and the admitted evidence side by side. It is arithmetic on record numbers, not a power-flow study, and it does not claim to be one. Its point is narrower: once the record's own figures are applied, no study in this record shows what need remains for a third import path.
Table 1: The PBRP Load Measured Against the Record

Three points follow from the table.
First, the composition of the load. Of the 11,695 MW of non-oil-and-gas load in both PBRP cases, 61% rested on a TSP officer letter (55%) or was unconfirmed (6%), and 65% was cryptocurrency mining (59%) and data centers (6%). Applying the discount the Commission itself ordered for the 2025 RTP removes at least 3,571 MW. That reduction brings 2038 demand to no more than 22,829 MW, below the 23,659 MW the PBRP modeled for 2030, the year for which ERCOT studied only a 345-kV import path. The oil-and-gas half of the forecast fares no better. The ALJs found it "overstated and outdated."
Second, the size of the reduction against the size of the line. Applicants' sponsoring witness verified that the safe loading limit of a 765-kV line of this length "is approximately 2570 MW." The ALJs' minimum load reduction, 3,571 MW, is larger than that entire stated limit. Whether a reduction of that size changes flows on this line is a question for a power-flow study, and that is the study Applicants did not run. Its significance is that the record reflects a load adjustment larger than the line's stated safe-loading capability, yet Applicants identify no study rerunning the need analysis at that materially lower load. Applicants did not analyze whether Import Path 2 remains necessary at the adjusted load. They said instead that they "cannot speculate" about it.
Third, the direction of the remaining facts. The PBRP cites "the lack of conventional generation in the Permian Basin region" as a driving factor for the import paths. Since then, CPV's 1,350 MW combined-cycle plant at Basin Ranch has gone under construction with an expected 2029 start, supported by a Texas Energy Fund loan. The ALJs found that Texas Energy Fund projects alone account for 2,210 MW of new Permian generation expected before the 765-kV lines would be in service, and that generation in the basin "is actively being developed in the basin at a scale that rivals or exceeds the PBRP's projected load." Two data center complexes totaling 10,000 MW are being built with their own gas generation and no grid connection. Those loads were never in the PBRP forecast, so the table does not subtract them. They show where large new load is going.
The Legislature has pointed the same way. Senate Bill 6 requires large loads with on-site backup generation to disclose it, and allows ERCOT to direct those loads "to either deploy the customer's on-site backup generating facilities or curtail load" in an emergency. It also requires the Commission, when it approves a large load co-located behind the meter with existing generation, to keep that generation available to the grid in emergencies and allows it to require "customers to be held harmless for stranded or underutilized transmission assets resulting from the behind-the-meter operation." Staff's witness agreed that "bring your own generation, 2025 Texas Senate Bill 6 and off-grid installations have the potential to reduce forecasted load growth and decrease peak load potential," answering "Potentially." Every one of these facts post-dates the PBRP study cases, and none of them appears in a study that tests the need for these facilities.
Mr. Martin testified that all three paths are needed by 2030 "even if all 2,500 MW of planned dispatchable generation in the Permian Basin actually materializes." That testimony addresses only the 2,500 MW generation scenario Mr. Martin described. It does not address the adjusted load forecast together with the post-PBRP generation evidence the ALJs credited, and Mr. Martin did not run the studies behind his conclusion. If announced generation is to be discounted because it is not yet built, the same rule applies with more force to officer-letter load that is not yet under contract, which the Commission found has been coming into service at lower levels than claimed.
F.	The Far West import limits are operating constraints, and they do not make this line a requirement of any standard.
Applicants describe the Far West import generic transmission constraints (GTC) as system operating limits that ERCOT treats as interconnection reliability operating limits under NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4. FAC-011-4 is titled "System Operating Limits Methodology for the Operations Horizon," and its purpose is to ensure that operating limits "are determined based on an established methodology or methodologies." It applies to the Reliability Coordinator. It governs how operating limits are set. It does not direct what facilities are built.
The exit strategy Applicants cite was identified under ERCOT Nodal Protocol Section 3.10.7.6(7). It lists six projects for one constraint and eight for the other, and it lists "Permian Basin 765 kV Import Paths" as a single line item with a 2030 date. It does not identify a contingency, a violation, or an incremental effect for Bell County East to Big Hill. A protocol-based list of projects that would let ERCOT retire an operating limit does not show that one item on that list is required by a reliability standard. And Applicants' witness on this subject did not run the power flows that produced the list.
G.	A choice among import-path options that each addressed the identified violations is a comparative judgment, not a reliability requirement.
ERCOT "offered alternative 765 kV, 500 kV, and 345 kV import path options for the Commission's consideration." The 2024 RTP "developed two plans to address statewide reliability needs: the traditional 345-kV plan and the 765-kV plan," and it reports that "274 reliability projects were identified in the 2024 RTP's 345-kV plan to address all reliability violations." ERCOT's comparison found that "both the 345-kV and 765-kV transmission options provide significant advantages." The ALJs found that Applicants did not evaluate alternatives to the projects making up Import Path 2.
When a 345-kV plan also addresses every identified violation, the existence of that plan shows that the standard itself does not require this particular facility. The choice of the 765-kV plan may rest on transfer capability, efficiency, or cost. Those are reasons to prefer a facility. They are not proof that the facility is "necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards."
Applicants also say that "even at substantially reduced loads, this 765 kV transmission line remains needed." The only reduced-load study the Directory cites is ERCOT's statewide sensitivity, which found that "major portions" of both plans "will still be needed" and priced each plan "under the sensitivity case including the Permian Basin Reliability Import Path." That sensitivity kept the import path in, did not say which portions remain needed, and did not isolate Import Path 2.
H.	Federal law does not require these facilities, and declining to certify them would violate no federal standard.
The Chairman asked the ALJs to identify the NERC standards at issue and to address "whether failure to comply with the relevant NERC standards would result in violation of federal law." The record identifies two: TPL-001-5.1, a planning standard, and FAC-011-4, an operations standard. Neither one requires a particular line.
When a planning assessment shows the system cannot meet TPL-001-5.1's performance requirements, "the Planning Assessment shall include Corrective Action Plan(s) addressing how the performance requirements will be met." The standard then lists examples of acceptable actions, from new or modified transmission and generation facilities, to Protection Systems and Remedial Action Schemes, to Operating Procedures, to "rate applications, DSM, new technologies, or other initiatives." A standard that offers a menu does not order one dish.
Congress said the same thing in the statute that authorizes NERC standards. A reliability standard is a requirement "to provide for reliable operation of the bulk-power system," and the same definition provides that "the term does not include any requirement to enlarge such facilities or to construct new transmission capacity or generation capacity." The statute "does not authorize the ERO or the Commission to order the construction of additional generation or transmission capacity." Independently, a decision not to certify these facilities would not establish or cause a violation of a federal reliability standard. If a deficiency exists, TPL-001-5.1 requires a corrective action plan; it does not require this particular facility. The record shows that more than one plan was available, including ERCOT's own 345-kV plan.
Applicants also cite the ERCOT Planning Guide and Nodal Protocols. The Directory does not identify any provision of either that requires these particular facilities. On this record, the answer to Issue No. 11 is that the Bell County East to Big Hill facilities have not been shown to be necessary to meet any state or federal reliability standard.
I.	Applicants' reply to Intervenor's exceptions confirms that no study tested whether this line is required.
Applicants answered Intervenor's exceptions on need in their September 9 reply. Their answers are best read in their own words, because each one confirms the gap that Issue No. 11 asks the ALJs to address.
First, Applicants describe the studies on which they rely: "ERCOT's 2024 and 2025 RTPs modeled systemwide resources and power flows through Central Texas, including the Bell County East interface, with the 765 kV import paths. These planning models assume that the Import Path 2 Projects are in service and, under that assumption, demonstrate adequate power flows through the modeled network." A model that works with the line in it shows that the line can be operated. It does not show that the system fails without it. Issue No. 11 asks the second question.
Second, Applicants state the test they believe applies: "The relevant planning question is whether the proposed facilities will improve transfer capability and system reliability under the modeled power flow cases." Their exceptions put it more plainly: "The need for a specific transmission improvement is established by demonstrating that it outperforms other alternatives under the applicable planning criteria." Improvement and ranking are how one chooses the better of several facilities. The exemption from the economic tests reaches only "a transmission line that is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards." Applicants' own quotation of the 2024 RTP shows that ERCOT "developed two transmission plans (345-kV and 765-kV)" to address the same statewide reliability needs. A facility that outperforms other options that also meet the planning criteria is the preferred option. That is the showing Applicants describe. It may establish a preference among alternatives. It does not establish that this facility is necessary to meet a reliability standard.
Third, Applicants say a partial-build study "would test a different system from the one ERCOT and the Commission evaluated and is not required by PURA or the Commission's rules." The system without these facilities is the very system Issue No. 11 asks about. Intervenor does not contend that PURA or the Commission's rules prescribe a particular study. Applicants must still identify record evidence that these facilities are necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard, and none of the studies they cite identifies a violation attributable to their absence.
Fourth, Applicants say that no party has addressed ERCOT's "subsequent statements on the need date for Import Path 2," and they list five. Each one appears in this record, and each one either assumes Import Path 2 is in service or groups it with other projects. Applicants quote ERCOT's July 2024 transmittal letter as saying the 2024 RTP evaluation "could reveal a set of EHV solutions for 2030 needs in the Permian Basin." The letter says "it is possible that this evaluation could reveal" such solutions, and its next sentence ties the EHV option to 2038: "if the Commission is inclined to adopt an EHV solution to meet the 2038 Permian Basin load forecast, it may wish to defer a final decision on the import path options until the 2024 RTP has been finalized." A stated possibility is not a finding of need. The 2024 RTP's core plan began from a case that already contained all three import paths, as Section II.D shows. Applicants describe the 2025 RTP as carrying the three paths "in its base assumptions," which is the right word. Applicants describe ERCOT's December 2025 approval of other 765-kV projects as approval of projects "which depend on the Import Path 2 Projects being in service." A later project that assumes this line will be built does not show that this line is required. It shows that the assumption has been carried forward. And the April 2026 exit strategy lists the three import paths as one item, on studies Applicants' witness did not run, as Section II.F shows.
Applicants' witness also testified that "ERCOT has stated since at least December 2024 that all three import paths are needed by 2030." ERCOT's December 12, 2024 letter on sequencing, in which ERCOT addressed the timing of the import paths directly, says that "two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030." The record does not contain a later ERCOT study that removes Import Path 2 and reverses that statement.
Fifth, Applicants invoke "the great weight that must be given to ERCOT's recommendation," and they describe the governing rule as containing a "substantiation requirement." That requirement is the condition the ALJs found unmet. They found that the PBRP recommendation is not "substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth" and should not receive great weight under the rule. Great weight also attaches only to what ERCOT actually recommended. ERCOT never studied these facilities at the adjusted load, so it never recommended them as necessary at that load.
Sixth, Applicants point to "thermal overloads, voltage instability, and unsolvable power flow contingencies in both the 2030 and 2038 base cases under N-0 (system intact) conditions." For 2030, ERCOT's answer to those conditions was a 345-kV import path; it "considered only a 345-kV import path option." Both cases were built on the PBRP load that the ALJs found must be reduced by at least 3,571 MW. Violations in a case built on load this record does not support cannot show that this line is required.
Applicants also say that the net generation position of Central Texas is not "the relevant inquiry for a reliability project." Applicants' own Application describes the import paths as upgrades "needed to facilitate bulk power transfer to reliably serve the Permian Basin region." The ALJs found that "[w]ithout evidence of surplus available generation at the source end of the line, Applicants failed to show that Import Path 2 can perform its asserted function."
Finally, Applicants say the PFD "principally relies on lay testimony to second-guess ERCOT." This brief does not ask the ALJs to prefer lay opinion to ERCOT's engineering. Every point in it rests on ERCOT's own documents, Applicants' exhibits and discovery answers, the sworn testimony of Applicants' witnesses, and Applicants' own pleadings. The gap is in Applicants' proof, and Applicants' own words describe it.
III.	PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 13: THE RECORD CONTAINS NO ESTIMATE OF CONGESTION COST SAVINGS FROM THESE FACILITIES.
A.	Applicants chose the reliability label, and the exemption it carried now depends on Issue No. 11.
The PFD found that "the record contains no evidence quantifying either" the cost to consumers or the congestion cost savings. That finding followed Applicants' own choice. They told the ALJs that Import Path 2 "is a Reliability Project, Not an Economic Project" and that "reliability projects are expressly exempt from the economic tests, including the congestion cost savings test."
The exemption reaches only "a transmission line that is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards." The ALJs have already found that the record does not establish that Import Path 2 is needed for reliability, or that it is needed in 2030. As the Chairman explained, "[i]f the ALJs find that the transmission line fails to establish need as a reliability project, the question remains of whether need was demonstrated as an economic project." FoF No. 225, which treats the Project as a reliability project, should be revised to match the ALJs' own findings. Proposed replacement text appears in Section IV.
B.	The Directory's figures compare two statewide plans, not these facilities to their absence.
Applicants answer a project-specific question with portfolio-level numbers. A comparison of two portfolios measures something else. Every forward-looking figure in the Directory's Issue No. 13 section compares the statewide 765-kV plan to the statewide 345-kV plan. Issue No. 13 asks for the savings that "may result from the proposed transmission facilities," considering "the ability of the proposed transmission facilities to reduce those congestion levels." The Commission's test asks whether "the levelized ERCOT-wide annual congestion cost savings attributable to the proposed project" meet the required threshold. You cannot measure a fence post by the length of the whole fence. The difference between two statewide portfolios is not an estimate of what one segment of one of them saves. No entry in the Directory assigns any part of the plan-level results to these facilities, or compares the system with them to the system without them.
The 2025 RTP's congestion figures carry the same defect. Its economic cases "used the 2024 RTP final reliability cases as the start cases, specifically the 2027 summer peak case and the 2030 summer peak case with the 765-kV - STEP incorporated." A congestion study that begins with the facility in place cannot estimate the congestion the facility removes.
C.	Historical and systemwide congestion figures describe a problem; they do not estimate what these facilities would save.
The Directory also cites ERCOT-wide congestion rent for 2023 and 2024, the Independent Market Monitor's estimate of congestion costs from 2020 through 2024, and the existence of three costly constraints. Those figures describe existing congestion. None estimates the share these facilities would relieve, which is the second half of the question Issue No. 13 asks.
Oncor's own securities disclosure, admitted as Howton Ex. JAH-27, makes the point: "The STEP is designed to mitigate some of this congestion. However, there is no guarantee that the execution of STEP and the PBRP will eliminate or reduce the amount of congestion within the ERCOT system." A company that tells investors its program may not reduce congestion has not estimated, for consumers, the congestion savings these facilities would produce.
D.	The findings PURA § 37.056(d) requires cannot be made on this record.
For a transmission project in ERCOT "that is not necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards," the Commission's criteria "must include a comparison of the estimated cost of the transmission project for consumers and the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the transmission project." The Commission "shall include with its decision on an application for a certificate to which this subsection applies findings on the criteria." The PFD found that Applicants submitted the projected construction cost, "not the cost of the facilities to consumers," and that "the tariff exposure on steel and aluminum has not been analyzed." With neither the consumer cost nor the facility-specific savings in the record, the required comparison cannot be made. The answer to Issue No. 13 is that the record contains no estimate of the congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from these facilities. Without that evidence, Applicants cannot establish need under the criteria that apply when facilities are not necessary to meet a reliability standard.
IV.	PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW ON REMAND
Intervenor respectfully proposes the following findings of fact and conclusions of law for the supplemental proposal for decision.
Proposed Findings of Fact: Preliminary Order Issue No. 11
R-1.	The reliability standards identified in the record are NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, a transmission planning standard, and NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4, a standard governing the methodology for setting system operating limits in the operations horizon. ERCOT also applied the ERCOT Planning Guide and Nodal Protocols. Applicants' Ex. 1 (Application) at 21; Applicants' Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.) at 8-9; Directory at 3-14.
R-2.	The record contains no study that compares system performance with and without the Bell County East to Big Hill facilities and identifies a violation of TPL-001-5.1, by study case, study year, and contingency, attributable to their absence. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:17-45:4; Applicants' Exceptions at 26 (Item No. 6484); PFD at 88-89.
